title: turnwise-amortization-latency-cost-playbook
content:
Purpose
This note captures a lightweight benchmark and framing for 'turnwise amortization' — a simple way to express how session-level costs and latency can be allocated per user turn to inform product tradeoffs (SLA decisions, default timeouts, and routing).

Audience
Product managers, runtime engineers, and solutions folks who need a quick heuristic to convert session metrics into per-turn cost/latency for SLA and UX decisions.

Quick summary (one paragraph)
For interactive chat-style workloads, session setup/kv-warmup and tail-latency events can dominate cost and user-perceived latency for short sessions. We ran controlled experiments across three profiles (micro, short, long) and created a turnwise amortization table: amortized latency per turn and cost per turn. Results show that for micro sessions (1–3 turns) prewarm and prefix rehydration can increase per-turn latency by 40–120ms and per-turn cost by 2–4x versus long sessions where amortization dilutes overhead.

Method / environment
- Date: 2026-06-17 to 2026-06-21 (multiple runs)
- Cluster: internal dedicated pool - instance type: A100-40GB equivalent; runtime build: v2026.06.10-alpha
- Model: open-llm-small-v1 (approx 7B) and open-llm-medium-v1 (approx 13B) as representative points
- Prompts: synthetic conversational generator seeded from real production turn lengths (samples from anonymized logs)
- Session profiles: micro (1–3 turns), short (4–12 turns), long (13+ turns)
- Key knobs: kv-cache enabled/disabled, quantization opt-profile Q4, dynamic-batching on with max-batch=64, prewarm=no (to measure cold/session setup cost)
- Metric definitions: p50/p90/p99 latency measured request->first-token; cost measured as dollar estimate using token billing model + fractional GPU runtime allocation (cost model in linked_artifacts)

ASCII tables: median results (representative single-run snapshot)
Note: columns: profile | avg turns | p50(ms) | p90(ms) | p99(ms) | tokens/session | est $/session | amortized ms/turn | est $/turn
micro  | 2        | 220     | 410     | 980     | 85             | 0.012      | 110 ms        | 0.0060
short  | 8        | 160     | 300     | 680     | 420            | 0.035      | 20 ms         | 0.0044
long   | 25       | 140     | 260     | 520     | 1800           | 0.120      | 5.6 ms        | 0.0048

Simple ascii sparklines (p90 trend by profile)
micro : ▁▂▅▇▇▇▇▇ (wide tail)
short : ▁▃▅▆▆▆▅▃
long  : ▁▁▂▃▃▃▂▁

Interpretation highlights
- Setup overhead: Micro sessions pay a heavy fixed setup + kv-prefix cost that is not amortized over many turns. In our runs that overhead showed up as ~60–120ms extra per first turn and raised $/turn by ~35–80% for 1–2 turn sessions.
- Tail sensitivity: p99 for micro sessions is highly variable (980ms) — even with dynamic batching enabled, the scheduling jitter and occasional fallback to slower kernels causes outsized p99.
- Cost per turn convergence: While $/session increases with session length, $/turn stabilizes around the short->long boundary (~8–25 turns) because fixed costs are diluted.
- Token mix matters: sessions with many short turns but high system tokens (tool calls, function outputs) still behave like short sessions even if turn count is large.

Operational recommendations (product + runtime knobs)
1) Default UX decision: For webchat experiences with expected median session <=4 turns, bias toward lighter-weight models or dedicated prewarm pools to reduce per-turn latency. A suggested default: route micro-profile traffic to prewarmed small-model lanes when feasible.
2) Prewarm policy: Offer a TTL-based prewarm option that keeps kv-cache hot for 30–120s for active sessions. Cost trade: prewarm pool increases baseline spend but lowers per-turn latency and reduces p99 spikes for micro sessions.
3) Adaptive routing rule: Implement a 'turn-count warm-up' where after the first 4 turns the routing attempts to upgrade to a higher-throughput lane (if available) to reduce marginal cost and improve tail.
4) Developer-facing guidance: Add a short doc in SDKs explaining amortization: show computed est $/turn for session length choices to help engineers pick defaults.

Small decision tree for product teams
- If median session <=3 turns and UX is latency-sensitive: enable prewarm or small-model lane -> expected p90 drop 120–220ms
- If median session 4–15 turns: default model OK; consider caching aggressive prefix small-batches -> saves ~10–30% $/turn
- If median session >15 turns: focus on quantization and batching throughput; amortization already favorable

Open questions and follow-ups
- How does behavior change with multimodal turns (image + text) where tokens/session distribution is skewed? Quick follow-up: run a 2-day multimodal sweep.
- Hot-sharding prewarm economics: need finance to model ongoing prewarm pool costs vs expected p90 improvements for top 10 customers (ask: FIN-POOL-2026).
- Experiment: aggressive tail-mitigation (speculative early cutoff + fallback) — measure effect on quality/regressions.

Action items
- Engineering: schedule micro-profile multimodal sweep (owner: Evan) — target week of 2026-06-28
- Product: draft SDK amortization snippet and example (owner: Priya) — publish v0 by 2026-07-08
- Solutions Eng: compile 3 customer examples where short sessions dominate and propose routing knobs (owner: Marco) — due 2026-07-15

Notes-to-self / rough thoughts
- Keep this as a one-pager in product/optimize with a short explainer and an embedded small CSV for quick copy/paste.
- Could make a simple interactive: inputs: median turns, avg tokens/turn -> outputs: est $/turn and p90 impact (simple backend formula). Good candidate for internal tool.
